If Captchas are used to improve a bot's reading skill, What is the meaning of the 'tick-box' captchas that give you nothing to solve?

Image categorization to improve machine vision. You're labeling the images with "pasta" or "coffee" and so the machine learning algorithm can look at the common patterns among images of that category and then learn what the concept associated with "pasta" or "coffee" looks like.

This guy explains how machine learning can infer concepts from such images:
https://www.ted.com/talks/jeremy_howard_the_wonderful_and_terrifying_implications_of_computers_that_can_learn?language=en
You're misunderstanding me here. I'm talking about the captchas that require you to just tick a box, and I mean click it nothing else, in order to prove you're not a robot.

If you're talking about captcha like on 4chan, then this box ticking is just to confirm you're a human solving it, so google (recaptcha's owner) can show you the actual captcha and make you tag signs, house numbers and street names for google streetview and google earth, and train their alghorithms like u/toats accurately explained. In short - google needs free labour, and they want to make sure you can provide it.

Both of you are talking about the same CAPTCHA, reCAPTCHA's latest multi-step CAPTCHA.

First, you check the box. The CAPTCHA runs some JavaScript to decide whether you're likely to be on a legit browser on a legit OS on a legit IP and whether your box-checking behavior was organic. If it has high confidence per these factors, it authorizes you. If it doesn't, it gives you an image or text recognition puzzle, as described by @toats.

Captchas are primarily to distinguish between humans and bots to prevent spam.

Some popular captchas have the dual purpose of training/complementing optical character recognition.

The check box captchas are weak captchas that are basically just testing to see if you are using a normal browser.
